papers.title: A Unified Flexible Large Polysomnography Model for Sleep Staging and Downstream Clinical Screening
papers.abstract: Polysomnography (PSG) is central to sleep medicine, yet its analysis remains hindered by labor-intensive manual scoring and limited cross-center generalizability. We present LPSGM, a large-scale PSG model trained on 220,500 hours of data from 16 public datasets (24,000 recordings) that addresses two challenges: cross-center sleep staging generalization and PSG-based screening of narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and depression. LPSGM integrates domain-adaptive pre-training, flexible channel configurations, and a unified architecture to accommodate heterogeneous recording protocols. In prospective validation, LPSGM achieves expert-level sleep staging ({kappa} = 0.845 {+/-} 0.066 vs. inter-expert {kappa} = 0.850 {+/-} 0.102) and matches fully supervised models on independent private cohorts. For downstream screening, LPSGM achieves 84.2% accuracy ({kappa} = 0.761) in three-class narcolepsy classification, with cross-institutional transfer for normal-versus-abnormal hypersomnia yielding an AUC of 0.879. Severe OSA screening reaches an AUC of 0.874 without access to respiratory signals. Depression symptom screening achieves an AUC of 0.801 in a surrogate-labeled APPLES cohort, and cross-dataset transfer to an independent clinically diagnosed cohort reaches an AUC of 0.965. These results suggest that LPSGM's pre-trained representations capture sleep-related signatures that generalize across institutions and support PSG-based screening of clinically relevant conditions. The code and pre-trained model are publicly available at https://github.com/Deng-GuiFeng/LPSGM.

papers.title: Between- and Within-Person Coupling of Nocturnal Heart Rate and Glucose: Retrospective, Real-World Observational Study of 105,196 Nights From 2648 Adults Using Ultrahuman Ring and Continuous Glucose Monitoring
papers.abstract: Background: Higher resting or sleeping heart rate (HR) has been associated with poorer glucose metabolism in adults without diabetes. However, these associations were estimated across individuals, and within-person characterization of this co-regulation during naturalistic sleep in large free-living cohorts remains limited. Objective: This study aimed to determine whether average sleeping HR, an indirect index of cardiac autonomic tone, is associated with nocturnal glucose within a participant and between participants, and whether night-to-night irregularity in sleep duration, sleep onset, and wake time is associated with nocturnal glycemia. Methods: In this retrospective observational study, adults who concurrently wore an Ultrahuman Ring and a continuous glucose monitor between January 2024 and June 2025 were analyzed. After participant- and night-level filtering, the cohort comprised 2648 participants from 87 countries, contributing 105,196 paired nights. Each predictor was decomposed into within- and between-participant components by person-mean centering and entered a single linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept for participant, adjusted for age, body mass index (BMI), and sex. Outcomes were nocturnal mean glucose, nocturnal glucose coefficient of variation (CV), and nocturnal time in range (70-110 mg/dL). Per-participant slopes were fitted in participants with sustained wear (at least 30 nights spanning at least 60 days). Estimates were re-derived under trimming and robust-regression specifications and refitted within BMI and regional strata. Results: Higher average sleeping HR was associated with higher nocturnal mean glucose both within participants (+5.7 mg/dL per 10 bpm, 95% CI 5.4-5.9) and between participants (+6.5 mg/dL, 95% CI 5.6-7.3; both P<.001). Within participants, higher sleeping HR was also associated with higher glucose CV (+1.37 percentage points, 95% CI 1.30-1.43) and lower time in range (-6.3 percentage points, 95% CI -6.7 to -6.0). Of the 911 sustained-wear participants, 701 (76.9%, 95% CI 74.1%-79.6%) had a positive individual slope (median of +5.2 mg/dL per 10 bpm). The association survived in every BMI stratum and in all 5 regional strata. Sleep-duration irregularity was associated with mean glucose between participants (+4.1 mg/dL per 30 minutes, 95% CI 2.6-5.7) but only weakly within them (+0.23 mg/dL). Within participants, a night 1 standard deviation above a participants own mean sleeping HR corresponded to 2.5 mg/dL higher nocturnal mean glucose. Conclusions: Average sleeping HR was associated with glucose within individuals as well as between them, indicating that the relationship is not attributable solely to stable between-person differences and reflects, at least in part, night-to-night covariation. The association was modest, but discernible in naturalistic sleep across geographies. Sleep-duration irregularity was associated with nocturnal glycemia mainly between individuals.

papers.title: Diet Quality Scores are Associated with Sleep Timing and Regularity in Emerging Adults
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep health is associated with cardiometabolic health, potentially due to direct physiological effects, altered diet quality, or a combination of both. However, data on multidimensional sleep health, particularly sleep regularity and holistic dietary patterns, in emerging adults remain limited. Objective: To examine associations between sleep health and diet quality in emerging adults. Methods: Objective sleep (duration, efficiency, timing [bedtime, waketime, midpoint], regularity) was measured via actigraphy: n=106 (48M/58F, age [median = 22, IQR = 2] years, BMI [24.2, 4] kg/m2). Subjective sleep quality was measured via Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index: n=122 (58M/64F, age [22, 2], BMI [24.2, 5] kg/m2. We collected diet data via daily food and fluid diaries ([≥]3 days) to determine Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH; 0-9) and Healthy Eating Index (HEI; 0-100) scores. We used hierarchical regressions (model 1: bivariate analysis, model 2: sex, BMI, race) to examine associations between sleep health and diet quality. We compared diet quality between participants obtaining adequate and inadequate sleep for each sleep health metric using Mann-Whitney U tests. Results: Sleep midpoint and bedtime were independently associated with DASH (Bs [≥] -0.165, ps [≤] 0.001) and HEI (Bs [≥] -2.180, ps [≤] 0.001) after inclusion of covariates. Group comparisons indicated higher diet quality among participants with adequate sleep midpoint and waketime SD (p [≤] 0.040). Conclusions: Higher sleep regularity is associated with better diet quality in emerging adults. These relations may be bidirectional, thus future studies are needed to investigate whether sleep health interventions improve diet quality, or vice versa, among emerging adults.

papers.title: The Portland SEEQ: A Harmonizable Questionnaire for Environmental Exposome Profiling in Prodromal Synucleinopathy
papers.abstract: Objective: To describe development of the Portland Suspected Environmental Exposures Questionnaire (SEEQ) and its initial application for environmental exposome profiling in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD). Background: Environmental exposures may contribute to Parkinson disease and related synucleinopathies, yet existing instruments variably capture specific agents, co-exposures, exposure uncertainty, timing, and mitigating factors. Methods: SEEQ was iteratively developed to assess pesticides, solvents/industrial chemicals, welding fumes, heavy metals, residential and occupational exposures, and relevant lifestyle factors. Direct exposures were classified as definite, probable, possible, or uncertain/unlikely, with additional assessment of frequency/duration, life stage, and protective-equipment use. SEEQ was administered to participants with polysomnography-confirmed iRBD. Exposure prevalence, co-exposure patterns, and exploratory associations with clinical phenotypes and longitudinal progression were examined. Results: Eighty-three participants completed SEEQ; 81 (97.6%) completed all four direct exposure domains. Definite/probable exposure was reported for pesticides in 38.6%, solvents/industrial chemicals in 43.4%, welding fumes in 21.0%, and heavy metals in 34.1%. Among complete responders, 60.5% reported [≥]1 and 42.0% [≥]2 direct exposure domains. Forty-five participants identified [≥]1 named agent or mixture. Greater exposure burden was cross-sectionally associated most consistently with greater autonomic symptom burden, but was not associated with longitudinal clinical worsening. Conclusion: SEEQ provides a practical, multidomain framework for structured environmental exposome profiling in prodromal synucleinopathy. Larger studies with external exposure validation and longitudinal follow-up are needed.

papers.title: Strategies to establish a biologically defined Parkinson's disease cohort prior to the onset of clinically significant motor symptoms
papers.abstract: Identifying individuals at risk for neurodegeneration is a priority for clinical trials. Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI) deploys strategies to enroll individuals before typical clinical Parkinson's disease symptoms: recruiting polysomnogram-confirmed REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) and central identification of hyposmia via smell testing. Groups were divided into RBD with and without hyposmia (RBD+Hyposmia, RBD-Hyposmia) and hyposmia with and without self-reported dream enactment behavior (Hyposmia+DEB, Hyposmia-DEB). Participants underwent clinical and biomarker testing including CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (CSFaSynSAA) and dopamine transporter imaging. While all enrollment strategies showed robust enrichment for CSFaSynSAA positivity, RBD+Hyposmia and Hyposmia+DEB were more likely CSFaSynSAA+ (94% and 85%) vs RBD-Hyposmia (40%) and Hyposmia-DEB (55%). Among CSFaSynSAA+, RBD+Hyposmia and Hyposmia+DEB had more mood, autonomic, and cognitive symptoms than Hyposmia-DEB. PPMI identified a large biologically-defined early neuronal synucleinopathy cohort and demonstrated biomarker and multi-domain clinical heterogeneity within CSFaSynSAA+ individuals prior to symptom onset.

papers.title: Theta-band EEG changes following sequential rTMS and tACS in fibromyalgia: A randomized controlled pilot study
papers.abstract: Background: Sequential application of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) may induce neurophysiological changes within sensorimotor and pain-related networks. However, the resting-state EEG effects of this combined approach in fibromyalgia remain unknown. Methods: In this exploratory randomized controlled pilot study, 10 adults with fibromyalgia were assigned to active stimulation (n = 5) or a no-stimulation control group (n = 5). Active participants received one or two sessions of 10-Hz rTMS over the left primary motor cortex (1,000 pulses/session), followed by 10 daily sessions of bilateral 10-Hz tACS (1 mA, 20 min). Six-minute eyes-closed resting-state EEG recordings were obtained before and after the intervention or an equivalent control interval. Power spectral density was quantified in the delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands and analyzed using mixed repeated-measures ANOVAs across central-centroparietal and posterior regions of interest. Results: Theta power increased significantly in the active group but not in controls, yielding significant Time x Group (F(1,8)=8.70, p=.018, p2=.521) and Time x ROI x Group (F(1,8)=5.53, p=.047, p2=.409) interactions. Follow-up analyses showed increased theta power in both central-centroparietal (p=.004) and posterior (p=.012) regions, with a larger increase observed posteriorly. No significant interaction effects were found for delta, alpha, or beta power. Conclusions: Sequential motor-cortex rTMS followed by repeated bilateral 10-Hz tACS was associated with increased resting-state theta activity in fibromyalgia. Given the small sample size, post hoc ROI selection, lack of sham stimulation, and absence of component-specific control conditions, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require replication in adequately powered sham-controlled studies.

papers.title: 'Somebody to find an answer, so I can sleep at night': Diverse Perspectives on Genomic Research for Rare Disease
papers.abstract: Purpose: Rare disease genomic research suffers from the underrepresentation of minoritized populations. We therefore sought to elucidate equitable strategies for participant engagement in rare disease genomic research. Methods: Eligible participants had previously applied to the Rare Genomes Project (RGP) and are underrepresented in genomic research by virtue of race, ethnicity, language, socio-economic status, educational level, or rural status. We also recruited clinicians who have referred potential participants to RGP. We performed semi-structured interviews with all enrollees. Results: Analysis of the 41 interviews, including 25 RGP participants and 16 clinicians, yielded four primary themes: 1) rare disease genomic research studies are intertwined with clinical care and hold potential to overcome access barriers in the clinic, with subsequent equity implications, 2) research participation functions as a rare disease community resource, offering psychosocial benefit and access to emerging science, 3) flexibility in research processes allows for increased access for diverse participants, and 4) longitudinal engagement is strengthened through relational continuity with participants and their clinical team. Conclusion: Overall, the motivators and experiences shared by clinicians and diverse participants inform effective engagement in rare disease genomic research and highlight the importance of providing equitable access to genomic sequencing for rare disease diagnosis.

papers.title: A transient decrease in night-to-night variability of REM sleep before myocardial infarction
papers.abstract: Background. Myocardial infarction (MI) outcomes depend on time to treatment, and fatigue and sleep disturbance are often reported in the weeks before the event. Whether wearable-measured sleep changes within individuals before MI, and whether such change is specific to MI, is unknown. Methods. In the All of Us Research Program, adults with a first MI code and at least 180 valid Fitbit sleep nights in the preceding 360 days were matched to up to 10 controls on sex, comorbidities, sleep apnea, calendar time and a propensity score. The full matched cohort of all cases was the primary cohort, and cases with diabetes and/or hypertension formed a subgroup. The main endpoints were the within-person change in night-to-night variability (SD, RMSSD, CV) of the REM-sleep fraction at days 30-16 relative to each persons baseline (days 360-121) and from days 30-16 to days 15-1, tested against 10,000 randomly placed index dates with allowance for the choice of window (max-T). The same pipeline was applied to cases without recorded symptoms or treatment, to an index date at the first angina code, to a cohort including heart failure and to ischaemic stroke and admissions for heart failure, pneumonia, fracture or appendicitis and any cause, and the analysis was adjusted for nightly heart rate, wear and device. Results. The full matched cohort comprised 45 cases and 450 controls. REM-fraction variability changed transiently before MI, decreasing at days 30-16 and returning towards baseline over days 15-1; allowing for the choice of window, this decrease-then-return pattern was rarely matched at 10,000 randomly placed index dates (max-T p<0.001). Its components were the decrease in SD at days 30-16 (Cliffs {delta} -0.30, p=0.004; OR per SD 0.53, 95% CI 0.35-0.80; max-T p=0.0034) and the return in RMSSD over days 15-1 ({delta} +0.36, p<0.001; max-T p=0.0035); day by day, the decrease was not detected as a continuous change (cluster permutation test p=0.58). The decrease in SD was not seen at the same time before admissions for pneumonia (69 cases), fracture or appendicitis (130) or any cause (859) and was larger before MI than before each of them (difference in {delta} -0.25 to -0.34), whereas the rise over days 15-1 was shared with pneumonia; it was of similar size in the subgroup with diabetes and/or hypertension, in cases without recorded symptoms or treatment, with the index date at the first angina code, when people with heart failure were included and after adjustment for nightly heart rate, wear and device. Scoring each person against their own baseline discriminated cases from controls with AUCs of up to 0.66, probably an optimistic estimate because the decrease in RMSSD was attenuated in held-out halves of the matched sets. Conclusions. In adults who use consumer wearables, a first MI was preceded by a transient change in night-to-night REM-sleep variability, a decrease at days 30-16 and a return over the following two weeks. The decrease was not seen at the same time before other acute admissions, did not depend on recorded symptoms or treatment and was detectable against each persons own baseline with simple measures. The timing is an exploratory finding, to be confirmed in new cases.

papers.title: Diurnal Glycemic Redistribution in Obesity Despite Matched Mean Glucose
papers.abstract: Background and Aims: Mean glucose and HbA1c reflect average glycemic exposure but do not capture its 24-hour distribution. When average glycemia is comparable, whether obesity is associated with a distinct temporal glucose pattern remains unclear. We compared continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) profiles in lean adults and adults with obesity matched for mean glucose. Methods: In a cross-sectional AI-READI analysis, lean adults (BMI 18.5 to <25 kg/m2) were matched one-to-one to adults with obesity (BMI >=30 kg/m2) by recruitment center and clinical group, with calipers for age, mean glucose and glucose standard deviation. CGM profiles were compared by clock time and relative to wearable-defined sleep onset. Sensitivity analyses tightened mean-glucose calipers from 10 to 2 mg/dL. Results: Among 261 matched pairs, mean glucose (lean versus obesity: 122.34 versus 122.82 mg/dL) and HbA1c (5.73% versus 5.78%) were comparable. Obesity was associated with higher nighttime glucose (00:00-06:00; +6.18 mg/dL) and lower afternoon glucose (12:00-18:00; -5.11 mg/dL; both adjusted P<0.001). Sleep-aligned analyses supported the nocturnal pattern, including among healthy participants and those with prediabetes. These differences persisted with a 2 mg/dL mean-glucose caliper (nighttime +3.86 mg/dL; afternoon -4.27 mg/dL; both adjusted P<0.001). Conclusion: Despite comparable mean glucose and HbA1c, obesity is associated with diurnal glycemic redistribution, characterized by higher nocturnal and lower daytime glucose. These findings support examining glucose timing alongside conventional measures of average glycemia.
